analysis.one_liner: Adds prison terms and fines for knowingly or recklessly endangering life through environmental crimes.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered: introduced in July 1991 with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed through the end of the 102nd Congress in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add new federal crimes for polluters whose violations knowingly, recklessly, or negligently put people at risk of death, serious injury, or environmental catastrophe. Penalties would stack on top of the underlying pollution violation — up to 30 years in prison for repeat offenses and corporate fines up to $2 million. Courts would also be required to order companies convicted of felony environmental offenses to pay for an independent compliance audit and fix what it finds, and any private citizen could report noncompliance to the court.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near polluting facilities — the people most exposed to illegal toxic releases, contaminated water, and hazardous waste. The bill gives prosecutors tougher tools against corporate polluters and gives any resident standing to tell a court when a company ignores a court-ordered cleanup or compliance plan.

how_it_helps.text: Creates new felony-level crimes, punishable by up to 15 years for a first offense and up to 30 years for repeat offenses, for committing an environmental offense while knowingly or recklessly creating a risk of death, serious injury, or environmental catastrophe.

Requires courts, when sentencing a company for a felony environmental offense, to order it to pay for an independent compliance audit by an expert with no ties to the company's management, and to order the company to implement the audit's recommendations for preventing repeat violations.
Gives the prosecutor, the auditor, any government agency, or any private individual the right to present evidence to the court that a company failed to comply, letting the court impose sanctions.
Defines 'environmental catastrophe' to cover death or injury to 20% or more of a species' known population in an ecosystem, or habitat destruction that blocks viable breeding.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and individuals convicted of environmental crimes would face much larger fines (up to $1 million per offense for organizations, doubled for repeat offenses), longer prison terms for executives and managers, and the cost of court-ordered independent audits and remediation. Companies across sectors regulated by the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, hazardous waste, pesticide, and toxic-substances laws would bear new criminal exposure.

drawbacks.text: Tougher criminal penalties and mandatory audits raise compliance costs for regulated businesses — from manufacturers to waste handlers — and those costs can be passed to consumers or lead some facilities to close rather than upgrade.

The bill's penalties apply in addition to punishment for the underlying pollution violation, so a single incident could trigger stacked charges and fines; critics of strict environmental enforcement argue this raises the risk of disproportionate punishment for technical violations that escalate.
Allowing 'any private individual' to trigger court proceedings over alleged noncompliance could invite litigation burdens for companies even after sentencing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — deterring corporate conduct that puts lives and ecosystems at risk, and giving residents a direct channel to enforce court-ordered fixes — are significant for exposed communities. The costs fall mainly on firms that violate environmental laws, though compliance spending could raise prices modestly across regulated industries. The audit mechanism is a genuinely novel enforcement tool rather than pure penalty inflation. On balance, a serious attempt to strengthen environmental criminal law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in July 1991, read twice, and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it died without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Harris Wofford introduced S. 1605 on July 31, 1991, with no cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was recorded — no committee vote, no floor debate, no roll call — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies regulated under federal environmental laws are better off: the bill's tougher criminal penalties, mandatory audits, and citizen enforcement mechanism never took effect, so exposure for violations remained governed by the pre-existing statutes alone.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Polluting firms and regulated manufacturers (chemical, energy, waste handling, agriculture)
industries.note: The bill would have added new criminal exposure — long prison terms, million-dollar fines, and mandatory audits — on top of existing pollution penalties. Communities near these facilities would have gained an enforcement tool these companies did not have to answer to before.
Every felony-level environmental conviction would have required a court-appointed independent audit, creating a new, court-mandated market for qualified environmental auditors.
